name: Hassan Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Hassan. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on the reconsiderations team at the regional benefits centre on Mill Street, which is an old bank building with terrible heating. When someone's jobseeker payment gets stopped or refused, they can ask us to look again, so I read the file, the evidence and the original decision, and I either uphold it or overturn it. I do maybe six or seven of those a day, plus calls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy finding the thing the first decision missed, like a sick note that was scanned upside down. I use AI tools every day, I've got my own templates that pull the timeline out of a messy file in two minutes, and I'm on the office's digital pilot group. What drains me is the backlog, we're sitting at about four hundred open cases, and the people waiting are often on nothing in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, fine, the tools are useful, let's use them properly and stop pretending they're magic. Online I'd probably post something on the pilot group's channel about which bits actually saved time. With friends I wouldn't bring it up, they'd be bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's basically the world I already live in. My templates save me maybe an hour a day, and in this picture that's as good as it gets. If AI is mostly hype, I've just got a slightly faster way to read four hundred angry files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am, and push the pilot group to roll my timeline template out to the whole team so the backlog comes down. I'd keep putting about two hundred and fifty a month into savings, I've got roughly three months put by. I might go for the senior caseworker post that's coming up in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The job is steady, the pay is fine, and I'm good with the tools. The only thing that bugs me is the backlog, which is a staffing problem, not an AI problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the backlog bugs you. Does it affect you personally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does when I'm on the phone with someone who's had no money for six weeks. I had a man last month who'd sold his bike to buy food while he waited for us. You go home and think about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the senior post change anything for you money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two thousand a year more, which would let me move out of the flat share with Jonas, my flatmate. That's the goal, honestly, my own place with a door that shuts.

say: I'd tell colleagues to use the tools **properly** and stop treating them as magic.
I'd post on the **pilot group** channel about what actually saved time.
think: This is basically the world I **already live in** with my templates.
The real problem is the **backlog of four hundred** cases, which is about staffing.
do: Push for my **timeline template** to roll out across the reconsiderations team.
Keep saving **two hundred and fifty** a month towards three months' cushion.
Apply for the **senior caseworker** post coming up in spring.
feel: **Calm**, because the job is steady and he is good with the tools.
S0.quote: If AI is mostly hype, I've just got a slightly faster way to read four hundred angry files.
fieldNote: He already uses AI **every day** and sees the plateau as no change.
His stress comes from claimants **waiting without money**, not from technology.
His money goal is modest: **his own flat** instead of a flat share.

steps.text: Push to roll out his timeline template across the team
Apply for the senior caseworker post in the spring
Keep saving two hundred and fifty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work this is our chance to clear the backlog and actually answer people in days instead of months. Online I'd be one of the people saying it can be done fairly if caseworkers help design it. With friends I'd be a bit more careful, because I know it sounds like I'm cheering for job cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm on the right side of it. Reading a file and drafting a decision letter are exactly the thinking tasks on that card, and the team will shrink. The people who build the new process keep their jobs, and the people who wait to be trained on it don't. I'd rather be building it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to lead the trial of the decision-drafting tool on our team, starting this quarter. I'd write up the rules for when a human has to check a case, like any case with a health condition. I'd also do a short online course in data protection law, because whoever understands the legal limits gets listened to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. I'd be fine, but I'd be the guy who helped make the tool that meant Priya's contract wasn't renewed. That's not a nice feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's Priya, and why her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya sits opposite me and we eat lunch together most days. She's on a fixed-term contract and she's slower with the tools, so she's exactly who doesn't get renewed. I'd try to pull her into the trial with me so she's not the one left out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're on the right side of it. Is that certain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, nothing's certain, but I'd bet on it. Government moves slowly and someone has to sign decisions legally, so I think caseworkers who run the tools last a good while. If I'm wrong, I'm twenty-seven with no kids, I can move.

say: I'd say at work this is our chance to **clear the backlog** in days, not months.
I'd argue online it can be done **fairly** if caseworkers help design it.
think: I think the team shrinks, but I'm **on the right side** of it.
Someone still has to **sign decisions legally**, so tool-running caseworkers last longer.
do: Volunteer to lead the **decision-drafting trial** on the team this quarter.
Write the rules for when a **human must check** a case.
Take a short online course in **data protection law**.
feel: A little **uneasy**, mostly guilt about colleagues like Priya losing out.
S1.quote: The people who build the new process keep their jobs, and the people who wait to be trained on it don't.
fieldNote: He is **confident** his own role survives because he'll run the tools.
His discomfort is **moral**, about helping cut colleagues' jobs.
He leans on **youth and no children** as his safety net.

steps.text: Lead the decision-drafting tool trial on the reconsiderations team
Bring Priya into the trial so she learns the tool
Complete a short online course in data protection law

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say people who've lost their benefits deserve a human who can explain the decision, and that has to stay in the law. At work I'd say it too, to my manager Karen. Online I'd be arguing about it a lot, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job as it is now is gone. AGI by 2028 means the machine reads the file better than I do, and my whole day is reading and deciding, there's no hands-on part to hide in. Being good with AI tools only helps until the AI doesn't need anyone to hold it. The question is whether the law keeps a human signature for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move straight onto whatever team oversees the AI decisions, because that's where the last human jobs in the office will be. I'd push my savings from three to six months by dropping the gym and cooking more. I'd also start freelance work on weekends, helping small charities set up their own AI tools, so I've got a second income before 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. I'd rather be doing ten things than sitting still. The two years would go very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot part, three years later, matter to you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for my job, I don't do anything with my hands at work. It matters for where I'd go next. If I thought about becoming an electrician like my cousin, I'd only get about three years before robots catch up, so that's not much of an escape for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Karen in that first meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say put me on the oversight team and let me write the checks, because I already know where the tools go wrong. Then I'd ask her straight out how many of us she thinks are left by 2029. She probably wouldn't know, which would tell me something.

say: I'd say claimants deserve **a human** who explains decisions, written into the law.
I'd raise it with **Karen**, my manager, and argue about it online.
think: My job as it is now is **gone by 2028**; it's all reading and deciding.
My **AI skills** only help until the AI needs nobody to hold it.
do: Move onto the team that **oversees AI decisions** as soon as it exists.
Build savings from three to **six months** by cutting the gym.
Start **weekend freelance work** setting up AI tools for small charities.
feel: **Anxious but busy**, preferring action to sitting still.
S2.quote: Being good with AI tools only helps until the AI doesn't need anyone to hold it.
fieldNote: He admits his **tool skills** stop protecting him once AI works alone.
He rules out a **trade** because robots arrive only three years later.
His hope rests on the law keeping a **human signature**.

steps.text: Ask Karen for a place on the AI oversight team
Cancel the gym and cook more to reach six months' savings
Set up AI tools for small charities on weekends for pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this to anyone who'd listen: we've got five years, start redesigning the office now and retrain people while they're still paid. Online I'd write longer posts, maybe even a blog. With friends I'd mostly ask what they're planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me room to get a qualification that matters. I'm thinking about a part-time law conversion course, because appeals tribunals and benefit rights advice still need people who can argue a case. My caseworker job still goes around 2031, but I'd be ready by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the law conversion course next September, evenings and weekends, about two years. I'd ask the office to pay part of the fees, they have a small training budget. I'd also put a bit into a low-cost index fund each month, because if AI companies win, I want a slice of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still, because the end point is the same. But it's the kind of anxious that gets you up early. I'd have a plan with dates on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd invest in index funds. Isn't that betting on the thing that takes your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit, and I know how it sounds. I'd rather own a tiny piece of the machine that replaces me than just be replaced. It's fifty a month, it's not going to make me rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about the law plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone has the same idea. If thousands of caseworkers all retrain as advisers at once, there's a queue for every job. That's why I'd start early instead of in year four.

say: I'd urge everyone to **retrain staff** while they're still being paid.
I'd write **longer posts**, maybe a blog, about redesigning the office.
think: Five years is enough for a **qualification that matters**.
Appeals tribunals and **rights advice** still need people who argue cases.
do: Start a part-time **law conversion course** next September, about two years.
Ask the office to cover part of the **fees** from its training budget.
Put **fifty a month** into a low-cost index fund.
feel: **Anxious**, but the kind that gets you up early with a dated plan.
S3.quote: I'd rather own a tiny piece of the machine that replaces me than just be replaced.
fieldNote: Five years shifts him from **holding on** to retraining for a new field.
He openly names the **contradiction** of investing in what replaces him.
His worry is a **crowded field** when every caseworker retrains at once.

steps.text: Start the part-time law conversion course next September
Ask the office training budget to cover part of the fees
Invest fifty a month in a low-cost index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and the government shouldn't waste it on reports. At work I'd push for every caseworker to get a training plan. Online I'd keep it practical, sharing courses that actually lead somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, with a whole career built on top of this one. I'd still expect the caseworker job to vanish around 2036. But I'd have time to become a qualified welfare rights adviser or even a tribunal judge's assistant, something higher up the chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same law course, but I'd take it slower and do it properly, and maybe the full qualification after. I'd go for the senior caseworker post first, because a few more years of senior pay helps fund the training. I'd also finally get my own flat, since a decade of steady pay makes that safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not much more. It's the same end point, but it feels like a change of career, not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything make you stay as a caseworker the whole time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the job changes into running the tools for a whole region. I'd stay a caseworker for ten more years only if the job turned into checking the machine instead of being checked by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jonas, your flatmate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas does accounts for a builders' merchant, so he's even more exposed than me. I'd tell him to start thinking now and not wait for year eight. He'd probably say I'm being dramatic, he always does.

say: I'd say ten years is **a gift** the government shouldn't waste on reports.
I'd push for every caseworker to get a **training plan**.
think: At **thirty-seven** I could have a whole new career built on this one.
I could become a **welfare rights adviser**, higher up the chain.
do: Apply for the **senior caseworker** post to fund the training.
Take the law course **slowly**, then the full qualification.
Rent **my own flat**, since steady pay makes it safe.
feel: Only **uneasy**; it feels like a career change rather than a disaster.
S4.quote: I'd stay a caseworker for ten more years only if the job turned into checking the machine instead of being checked by it.
fieldNote: With a decade he sees a **step up**, not an escape.
He links staying to the job becoming **checking the machine**.
He worries more for his **flatmate Jonas**, who does accounts, than for himself.

steps.text: Apply for the senior caseworker post for higher pay
Take the law conversion course slowly, then qualify fully
Move out of the flat share into a rented flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because even being good with the tools doesn't buy much time. What would help is a clear legal rule that a human signs off any decision that stops someone's money. If a machine can stop a person's benefits, a person should still have to put their name on that decision.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who gets the savings. If the office saves millions by automating, I'd want some of it going into faster payments for claimants and training for staff. Otherwise it just disappears into next year's budget cuts.

headlineQuote: If a machine can stop a person's benefits, a person should still have to put their name on that decision.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old reconsiderations caseworker** at a regional benefits centre, reviewing stopped jobseeker payments.
He uses AI **every day** and sits on the office's digital pilot group.
He is **pragmatic and adaptive**, single, sharing a flat and keeping about three months' savings.
He stays calm or uneasy in milder pictures, but turns **anxious** once AGI arrives within five years.
His long plan is a **law conversion course** towards welfare rights advice.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because **tool skills** buy very little time.
whatWouldHelp: A **legal rule** that a human signs any decision stopping someone's money.
